title: Antibiotic Side-Effect Reporting: Intolerance, Allergy, C. diff, or Toxicity?
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Antibiotic adverse effects are not interchangeable. Mild nausea differs from IgE-type allergy, severe cutaneous reaction, C. difficile diarrhea, organ toxicity, or drug interaction. Accurate description and rapid escalation of dangerous patterns protects the patient and prevents inaccurate allergy labels.
recognize: Hives, wheeze, angioedema or hypotension suggest immediate hypersensitivity; blistering rash/mucosal injury suggests severe cutaneous reaction.
New significant diarrhea during or after antibiotics raises C. difficile concern, especially in high-risk patients.
priorities: Describe the reaction, timing and drug precisely rather than writing only 'allergy.'
Stop and escalate immediately for anaphylaxis or severe cutaneous reaction according to emergency protocol.
Report clinically significant diarrhea, jaundice, tendon/neurologic symptoms, arrhythmia symptoms or other drug-specific toxicity.
assessMonitor: Monitor rash, airway, GI symptoms, hydration, fever, drug-specific labs and interacting medications.
interventions: Use isolation/contact precautions for suspected C. difficile according to facility protocol while evaluation proceeds.
medicationSafety: CDC notes antibiotic side effects range from common GI/rash symptoms to C. difficile and life-threatening allergic reactions; unnecessary antibiotics still carry those harms.
Do not relabel predictable intolerance as anaphylaxis without a clear history.
teaching: Report the exact reaction and timing; do not save/share leftover antibiotics or stop early without guidance unless a serious reaction requires urgent care.
delegationScope: PNs may monitor/administer antibiotics within scope and report adverse effects; emergency reactions require immediate escalation and protocol activation.
examTrap: Calling every episode of diarrhea a penicillin allergy instead of distinguishing intolerance, C. difficile risk and true hypersensitivity.
oneLinePearl: Describe the reaction before you name the allergy.
sourceBasis: CDC Antibiotic Use and Stewardship 2025 update published 2026
CDC antibiotic side-effect and penicillin-allergy guidance current 2026

title: Angina for the U.S. PN: Stable Pattern or Acute Coronary Syndrome?
bottomLine: The critical PN decision is whether chest discomfort matches the patient's known stable pattern and responds to the established plan or is new, worsening, prolonged, occurring at rest, or accompanied by instability—features that require urgent ACS evaluation.
recognize: Predictable exertional discomfort relieved by rest/antianginal plan can fit chronic angina.
New/rest pain, increasing frequency/severity, diaphoresis, dyspnea, nausea, syncope or hemodynamic change increases concern for ACS.
priorities: Stop exertion, assess symptoms/vitals and follow the ordered chest-pain plan.
Escalate immediately for new/worsening or unstable features rather than waiting for routine reassessment.
assessMonitor: Characterize onset, provocation, quality, radiation, severity, duration, associated symptoms and response to treatment.
interventions: Administer prescribed antianginal therapy within scope and reassess promptly; activate emergency response when indicated.
medicationSafety: Before nitrates, screen for hypotension and relevant PDE-5 inhibitor use according to the medication plan; do not improvise repeated dosing beyond orders/protocol.
teaching: Know the difference between the usual stable pattern and symptoms that require EMS/urgent evaluation.
delegationScope: PNs may perform focused data collection and ordered treatment; new or unstable chest pain requires RN/provider/emergency escalation.
examTrap: Reassuring the patient because the pain resembles prior angina even though it now occurs at rest and is lasting longer.
oneLinePearl: Stable angina is predictable; a changing pattern is unstable until proven otherwise.

title: The 5 Ps of Labor: Find What Is Slowing Progress
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Labor progress reflects interaction among passenger, passageway, powers, position and psyche. The PN uses the framework to organize observations, support comfort and mobility when appropriate, and report abnormal progress or fetal/maternal changes—not to diagnose dystocia independently.
recognize: Contraction pattern, fetal position/presentation, pelvic/soft-tissue factors, maternal position and anxiety/support can influence labor experience and progress.
A prolonged or abnormal pattern must be interpreted by the obstetric team in context of stage, parity, fetal status and interventions.
priorities: Observe contraction pattern, maternal coping/position and fetal status.
Support position changes/ambulation when allowed and safe.
Report concerning lack of progress or maternal/fetal deterioration.
assessMonitor: Trend contraction frequency/duration, cervical findings supplied by authorized examiner, fetal status, pain/coping, bladder status and maternal vitals.
interventions: Promote comfort, hydration/voiding per plan and frequent position changes compatible with monitoring/treatment.
medicationSafety: Oxytocin and analgesia can alter contraction pattern or maternal/fetal status; follow protocol and escalate tachysystole or instability.
teaching: Explain that labor progress depends on several interacting factors and position changes may improve comfort and mechanics when safe.
delegationScope: PN obstetric assessment/procedure authority varies; report findings to RN/provider and do not independently diagnose arrest disorders.
examTrap: Assuming weak progress is always caused by inadequate contractions without considering passenger, passageway and position.
oneLinePearl: Labor is five moving parts, not one cervix number.
sourceBasis: ACOG First and Second Stage Labor Management CPG No. 8

title: Fetal Positions: Translate the Letters Into Labor Mechanics
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Fetal position describes the relationship of the presenting landmark to the maternal pelvis. For exam reasoning, identify presentation and denominator first, then left/right and anterior/posterior; do not memorize letters without picturing the fetus in the pelvis.
recognize: Occiput anterior positions generally align favorably for vaginal birth; persistent posterior/transverse positions may increase back pain or slow descent but do not automatically mandate operative birth.
priorities: Use documented obstetric findings to anticipate comfort needs and labor progress.
Support position changes when appropriate and report abnormal descent or fetal-status concerns.
assessMonitor: Monitor labor progress, maternal pain location, fetal heart tracing and response to position changes.
interventions: Assist with lateral, upright, hands-and-knees or other approved positions based on comfort, monitoring and clinical plan.
medicationSafety: Neuraxial analgesia may limit mobility and requires fall/motor-block precautions.
teaching: Position labels describe where the fetal landmark points within the maternal pelvis.
delegationScope: PNs may reinforce interpretation already established by the obstetric team; determining presentation/position by invasive exam is jurisdiction/facility dependent.
examTrap: Reading 'LOP' as a diagnosis of obstructed labor rather than a position requiring clinical context.
oneLinePearl: Find the landmark, then map it to the maternal pelvis.

title: Mechanisms of Labor: Follow the Fetal Head Through the Pelvis
bottomLine: The cardinal movements—engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, restitution/external rotation and expulsion—describe how the fetus adapts to the pelvis. They are a physiologic sequence, not a checklist the nurse causes.
recognize: Descent and rotation occur across labor rather than in perfectly isolated steps.
Failure of descent/rotation must be interpreted in context of contractions, position, pelvic factors and fetal status.
priorities: Support maternal positioning and comfort while monitoring maternal/fetal response.
Report abnormal progress or fetal compromise.
assessMonitor: Trend documented station/position, contraction pattern, fetal status and maternal coping.
interventions: Assist with approved position changes and bladder emptying/comfort measures that may support labor mechanics.
medicationSafety: Analgesia/oxytocin can influence mobility or contraction pattern and require protocol-based monitoring.
teaching: Explain that the fetus normally rotates and flexes/extends to move through the pelvis.
delegationScope: PNs monitor and support within obstetric policy; diagnosis of labor arrest and operative decisions belong to the RN/provider/obstetric team.
examTrap: Treating the cardinal movements as rigidly separate events that must occur in a memorized minute-by-minute order.
oneLinePearl: The fetus rotates to fit the pelvis as descent continues.

title: True Labor vs Prelabor: Change Over Time Matters
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: True labor is defined by a pattern of contractions associated with progressive cervical change, not by pain intensity alone. Prelabor contractions may be uncomfortable yet irregular and nonprogressive; bleeding, fluid leakage, decreased fetal movement or maternal/fetal instability override the simple true-versus-false-labor question.
recognize: Contractions becoming regular/stronger/closer with progressive cervical change support true labor.
Rupture of membranes, significant bleeding, severe constant pain or decreased fetal movement requires obstetric evaluation regardless of contraction pattern.
priorities: Assess contraction pattern, membrane status, bleeding, fetal movement/status and maternal symptoms.
Escalate red flags promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend contractions, maternal vitals, fetal status and documented cervical findings when obtained by authorized staff.
interventions: Provide hydration/comfort and discharge teaching only when the obstetric team determines outpatient management is appropriate.
medicationSafety: Do not recommend sedatives, analgesics or tocolytics independently to 'test' whether labor is real.
teaching: Return/call for worsening regular contractions according to the plan, rupture of membranes, bleeding, decreased fetal movement or severe symptoms.
delegationScope: PNs may collect focused data and reinforce the established plan; diagnosis/disposition is obstetric-provider/RN directed.
examTrap: Using relief with rest as proof that a patient cannot be in true labor despite progressive cervical change.
oneLinePearl: Labor is a pattern plus cervical change; danger signs trump the label.
sourceBasis: ACOG First and Second Stage Labor Management CPG No. 8

title: Labor Breathing Techniques: Reduce Panic Without Hyperventilation
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Breathing techniques are coping tools, not a mandatory pattern. Encourage slow, comfortable breathing and relaxation; if rapid breathing causes lightheadedness, tingling or panic, coach slower breathing and reassess the patient rather than insisting on a rigid method.
recognize: Tense shoulders, breath holding, rapid shallow breathing, dizziness or perioral/finger tingling suggest ineffective coping or hyperventilation.
priorities: Stay calm, cue slow breathing and relaxation, and adapt to the patient's preferences/culture/support system.
Reassess pain and maternal/fetal status if coping suddenly deteriorates.
assessMonitor: Monitor pain/coping, respiratory pattern, anxiety, maternal vitals and fetal status as indicated.
interventions: Use focal points, counterpressure, position changes, partner coaching and rest between contractions as appropriate.
medicationSafety: Nonpharmacologic coping complements—not replaces—appropriate analgesia or evaluation of new severe pain.
complications: Missed clinical deterioration if symptoms are dismissed as anxiety
teaching: There is no single 'correct' labor-breathing pattern; use the technique that supports calm, effective ventilation and coping.
delegationScope: PNs may coach comfort measures within the plan; abrupt clinical changes require escalation.
examTrap: Assuming dizziness and tingling during very rapid breathing require oxygen before correcting hyperventilation and assessing the patient.
oneLinePearl: The goal is calm ventilation, not perfect counting.

title: Fetal Monitoring in Labor: Trace the Fetus and the Contractions Together
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Fetal monitoring evaluates fetal heart rate in relation to uterine activity and maternal condition. The PN should recognize concerning trends, reposition/support according to protocol, identify reversible causes and escalate rather than independently diagnosing or managing a persistent abnormal tracing.
recognize: Baseline, variability, accelerations and decelerations are interpreted together with contractions and clinical context.
A persistent concerning pattern or sudden prolonged change requires rapid team response.
priorities: Verify the signal and maternal pulse when artifact is possible.
Assess maternal position/vitals and contraction pattern.
Initiate approved intrauterine-resuscitative actions and notify RN/provider for concerning patterns.
assessMonitor: Trend fetal heart pattern, contractions, maternal BP/oxygenation, oxytocin exposure, membrane status and labor progress.
interventions: Position changes and correction of maternal hypotension or tachysystole are protocol-driven; oxygen is not a reflex treatment for every tracing abnormality.
medicationSafety: Oxytocin can cause uterine tachysystole and fetal compromise; follow facility stop/reduction and escalation protocols.
teaching: Explain what the monitors measure and that changes may prompt repositioning or other interventions.
delegationScope: Interpretation/management authority varies; PN should recognize, initiate authorized actions and escalate abnormal patterns promptly.
examTrap: Treating the fetal heart rate number alone without relating it to contractions, variability and maternal condition.
oneLinePearl: Read the fetal heart and the uterus as one conversation.
sourceBasis: ACOG Intrapartum Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring CPG No. 10, October 2025

title: FHR Variability: The Nervous-System Signal Inside the Tracing
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Baseline fetal heart rate variability reflects beat-to-beat autonomic interaction. Moderate variability is generally reassuring; minimal/absent variability must be interpreted with medications, fetal sleep, prematurity, hypoxia/acidemia risk and associated decelerations rather than labeled dangerous in isolation.
recognize: Variability can transiently decrease with fetal sleep or CNS-depressant medications.
Absent/minimal variability plus recurrent concerning decelerations or other deterioration increases urgency.
priorities: Confirm tracing quality and review maternal/fetal context.
Assess for hypotension, tachysystole, medication effects and other reversible contributors.
Escalate persistent concerning combinations.
assessMonitor: Trend variability with baseline, accelerations/decelerations, contractions, maternal vitals and medications.
interventions: Initiate protocol-approved supportive actions while notifying the RN/provider for persistent abnormal patterns.
medicationSafety: Opioids, magnesium and other CNS-active therapies may influence fetal heart characteristics; interpret in context rather than ignoring changes.
complications: Unnecessary intervention from overcalling a transient pattern
redFlags: Persistent absent variability with recurrent concerning decelerations
teaching: Explain that the team interprets the whole tracing over time, not one isolated feature.
delegationScope: PN role is recognition, authorized initial action and escalation; formal interpretation/management follows facility obstetric policy.
examTrap: Calling minimal variability automatically fetal hypoxia without checking sleep, medications and the rest of the tracing.
oneLinePearl: Variability is meaningful only in the context of the whole tracing.
sourceBasis: ACOG Intrapartum Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring CPG No. 10, October 2025

title: Four Stages of Labor: Know What Changes the Nursing Priority
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: The stages of labor organize nursing priorities: cervical change in stage one, birth in stage two, placental delivery in stage three, and immediate maternal recovery in stage four. The transition between stages changes what must be watched most closely, especially hemorrhage and maternal instability after birth.
recognize: Stage one progresses to complete dilation; stage two ends with birth; stage three ends with placental delivery; stage four is early recovery with high hemorrhage vigilance.
Heavy bleeding, boggy uterus, hypotension, severe pain or abnormal fetal pattern is never 'normal for the stage.'
priorities: Match assessments and support to the stage.
Maintain fetal surveillance during labor and hemorrhage surveillance after birth.
Escalate abnormal bleeding or maternal/fetal instability promptly.
assessMonitor: During labor trend contractions, fetal status and maternal vitals; after birth monitor fundus/bleeding, bladder, pain, vitals and recovery from anesthesia/analgesia.
interventions: Support comfort/positioning in labor and postpartum uterine/bleeding monitoring according to protocol.
medicationSafety: Uterotonics, analgesia/anesthesia and oxytocin require stage-specific monitoring and contraindication awareness.
teaching: Explain how nursing priorities shift from labor support and fetal monitoring to maternal hemorrhage/recovery surveillance after birth.
delegationScope: PN obstetric responsibilities vary by state/facility; unstable intrapartum or postpartum findings require immediate RN/provider escalation.
examTrap: Relaxing surveillance after the baby is born and missing stage-four postpartum hemorrhage.
oneLinePearl: Birth ends stage two—not the need for vigilant nursing care.
sourceBasis: ACOG First and Second Stage Labor Management CPG No. 8
